families.name: Rigid-Body Decomposition
families.definition: Methods that segment an object into distinct rigid parts and model their relative motion using joint parameters.

properties.text: These methods assume that each identified part moves as a single rigid body without internal deformation.
They typically rely on clustering algorithms or geometric priors to separate the object into components.
The kinematic structure is often represented as a tree or graph where edges denote joints.
This approach is computationally efficient for objects with clear, non-overlapping rigid segments.
It is particularly effective for mechanical objects like robots or vehicles with well-defined hinges.

limitations.text: The method fails when parts undergo significant non-rigid deformation, such as bending or stretching.
Segmentation errors can lead to incorrect part identification and subsequent motion modeling failures.
It struggles with objects that have complex, interpenetrating, or highly articulated structures.
The assumption of rigid parts limits applicability to soft or flexible materials.

families.name: Non-Rigid Articulation
families.definition: Approaches that model continuous deformations and flexible joints, allowing parts to bend or twist rather than just rotate.

properties.text: These methods use continuous deformation fields or spline-based representations to capture smooth motion.
They can handle objects with flexible limbs, such as tentacles or fabric-like appendages.
The kinematic model often involves higher-order derivatives to describe curvature and torsion.
This family is suitable for biological organisms or soft robotic systems.
It provides a more realistic representation of motion for objects that do not have discrete rigid segments.

limitations.text: The increased complexity leads to higher computational costs compared to rigid-body models.
Parameterizing the deformation field can be ill-posed without strong regularization or prior knowledge.
It is difficult to distinguish between true articulation and noise in the data.
The methods often require dense correspondence data, which is hard to obtain in practice.

families.name: Graph-Based Kinematics
families.definition: Techniques that represent the object's structure as a graph where nodes are parts and edges are joints, often learned from data.

properties.text: The graph structure encodes the topological relationships between different parts of the object.
Message passing or graph neural networks are often used to infer joint states from observations.
This approach allows for flexible and scalable modeling of complex hierarchical structures.
It can incorporate physical constraints directly into the graph edges.
The method is robust to variations in the number of parts or joints.

limitations.text: The quality of the model is heavily dependent on the accuracy of the learned graph structure.
It may struggle with objects that have dynamic or changing topologies.
The computational complexity can grow rapidly with the size of the graph.
It requires careful design of the message passing mechanism to ensure stability and convergence.

families.name: Deep Learning-Based Articulation
families.definition: Data-driven methods that use neural networks to learn the mapping from observations to articulated object states.

properties.text: These methods leverage large datasets to learn complex, non-linear relationships between input and output.
They can handle high-dimensional input data, such as point clouds or images, directly.
The models can implicitly learn the underlying kinematic structure without explicit parameterization.
This approach is highly flexible and can adapt to a wide variety of object types.
It often achieves state-of-the-art performance in benchmark tasks.

limitations.text: The methods require large amounts of labeled data for training, which is often scarce.
They lack interpretability, making it difficult to understand why a specific prediction was made.
The models may not generalize well to unseen object types or environments.
They are computationally expensive to train and deploy.
Developing robust methods for segmenting and modeling objects with both rigid and non-rigid parts simultaneously.
Improving the generalization of deep learning models to unseen object categories with limited data.
Integrating physical constraints and dynamics into learned articulation models to ensure physically plausible motion.
Creating efficient algorithms for real-time articulation modeling in dynamic and cluttered environments.
Establishing standardized benchmarks and datasets for evaluating articulation modeling methods across diverse object types.
